newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Plans to extend EU work time rules in difficulty.
newsitem.headline: Plans to extend EU work time rules in difficulty.

text.p: Senior European Commission officials are due on Thursday to try and patch up an internal row over plans to extend EU rules on working hours and rest times to workers not currently protected by the provisions.

The Commission had hoped to publish a discussion paper on Wednesday suggesting how the EU's Working Time Directive, which limits the average work week to 48 hours, should be applied to truck drivers, trainee doctors, offshore workers and others.
But senior Commission officials have rejected a draft text prepared by the services of Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flyyn, asking for it to be rewritten by tomorrow.

An aide to Energy Commissioner Christos Papoutsis told Reuters several Commissioners' cabinets had a problem with Flynn's ideas although all agreed protection needed extending to many of the nine million workers who are not currently covered.

For political reasons, Flynn wanted working time rules to protect workers across the board but he was also suggesting that problem areas should be covered by sector-specific arrangements, which was rather contradictory, the official said.

A member of Financial Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy's cabinet said the logic behind the across-the-board approach needed clarifying if it was to get the approval of EU Commissioners, who are due to examine the proposal next week.
A number of cabinets also had specific concerns about individual cases, particularly junior doctors, road hauliers and the workers in the offshore oil industry, officials said.
"If the directive is to cover all (sectors) it needs some serious derogations," Papoutsis's aide said.

He said the Greek Energy Commissioner would prefer the offshore oil sector to be left out altogether because its working patterns -- two or three weeks solid work followed by a fortnight's leave -- were incompatible with the directive.

In addition to setting a 48-hour week, the Working Time Directive limits night shifts to an average of eight hours and says everyone should have four weeks paid leave a year and at least one day off a week.

Commission and British officials said extending the rules to junior doctors posed genuine organisational and cost problems for the National Health Service (the NHS) in Britain, the only EU member state where trainee doctors are not self-employed.
The Working Time Directive only covers employees.
In general, though, Britain's new Labour government favoured extending the Working Time Directive, British diplomats said.
The previous Conservative administration in London brought and lost a court case against the 1993 law, claiming it had been adopted illegally.
